set1.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with a known red cell alloantibody is scheduled for elective hip surgery. When should her type and screen be ordered?
opts: Well before the surgery date
Correct. When a screen is positive, finding compatible antigen-negative units can take hours or days, so type and screen is ordered well in advance of elective procedures.
When she starts to bleed
Waiting for bleeding leaves no time to find antigen-negative units; order early for elective procedures.
After the crossmatch is done
The type and screen comes first; the crossmatch matches donor units after it, so it cannot come later.
On the morning of surgery
Same-day ordering leaves no time: with an alloantibody, compatible units can take hours or days to find.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 12 and 15

set1.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set1.q: A 68-year-old man of unknown blood type needs a massive transfusion after a fall. Which red cells are standard for him?
opts: AB-positive
Group AB red cells carry both A and B antigens and would be lysed by most recipients' antibodies; AB is the universal plasma donor.
O-negative
O-negative is scarce (about 6 to 7% of people) and is reserved for females of childbearing potential with an unknown type.
Type-specific units
His type is unknown and he is hemorrhaging; uncrossmatched group O units are released while the blood bank proceeds with rapid confirmatory testing.
O-positive
Correct. O-positive is abundant (about 37 to 39% of people) and is the massive transfusion standard for adult males and post-menopausal females.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 7

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 40-year-old man gets high fever, rigors, flank pain and red urine minutes into a transfusion. Which laboratory pattern is expected?
opts: Absent haptoglobin, high lactate dehydrogenase
Correct. Acute hemolytic reaction: undetectable haptoglobin, markedly elevated LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) and later a rise in indirect bilirubin, with pink or red plasma and red urine.
High tryptase with anti-IgA
High tryptase and anti-IgA mark anaphylaxis, which has no fever and normal hemolysis labs.
Normal haptoglobin and lactate dehydrogenase
Normal hemolysis labs fit the febrile non-hemolytic, allergic and anaphylactic reactions, not this triad of fever, flank pain and red urine.
Spherocytes with a new anti-Jka
Spherocytes and a new anti-Jka are the delayed hemolytic picture, 3 to 30 days after transfusion, not minutes.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 17 and 22

set1.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set1.q: A 42-year-old man's washed red cells agglutinate with anti-A, do not agglutinate with anti-B, and agglutinate with anti-D. What is his type?
opts: Group A, RhD-negative
Agglutination with anti-D means RhD-positive; an RhD-negative sample would show no reaction with anti-D.
Group B, RhD-positive
Group B cells would agglutinate with anti-B, not anti-A. His cells reacted with anti-A only.
Group A, RhD-positive
Correct. Forward typing reads antigens: agglutination with anti-A means the A antigen is present, no reaction with anti-B means no B antigen, and agglutination with anti-D means RhD-positive.
Group AB, RhD-positive
Group AB cells agglutinate with both anti-A and anti-B; his showed no reaction with anti-B.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 11

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 47-year-old man's transfusion has just been stopped for a suspected reaction. How is his intravenous access kept?
opts: Fresh saline through new tubing
Correct. Maintain intravenous access by hanging fresh normal saline with new tubing; never flush the remaining blood in the transfusion line into the patient.
Flush the old line with saline
Flushing the old line pushes the remaining blood into him; the tubing is replaced, not flushed.
Remove the catheter at once
Access is MAINTAINED for treatment; only the transfusion tubing is disconnected from the catheter hub.
Restart the unit more slowly
Restarting is allowed only for a purely skin-limited allergic reaction that fully resolves; here the blood is stopped and investigated.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 16 and 20

set1.io: Review Rh factor and incompatibility.
set1.q: A 31-year-old RhD-negative woman without anti-D has just delivered an RhD-positive baby. When should she receive Rh immune globulin?
opts: At her next prenatal visit
The window is within 72 hours of delivery; waiting for the next pregnancy leaves time for her B cells to respond to the fetal cells.
If the baby becomes jaundiced
The dose is routine after delivering an RhD-positive baby; it prevents her sensitization and does not depend on the baby's course.
Within 72 hours of delivery
Correct. The post-partum dose is given within 72 hours of delivering an RhD-positive neonate, adding to the routine dose at about 28 weeks.
Not needed after a first birth
Feto-maternal hemorrhage occurs during delivery or trauma, which is why the post-partum dose is given within 72 hours of delivery.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set1.q: A 61-year-old man's type and crossmatch has tagged and reserved 2 units, but surgery is canceled. What happens to the units?
opts: They are converted to plasma
Nothing converts red cell units; held units simply stay reserved until explicitly released.
They expire after 72 hours
The 72-hour limit applies to the patient's SAMPLE after recent transfusion or pregnancy, not to reserved units.
Nobody else can use them until released
Correct. Held units are unavailable to other patients until explicitly released, which is why a type and screen, which holds none, preserves inventory when transfusion is unlikely.
They go back to stock at once
Reserved units stay held until someone explicitly releases them; that is the stewardship cost of a crossmatch.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 15

set1.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set1.q: A 37-year-old woman's plasma agglutinates reagent A1 cells but not reagent B cells. What is her ABO group?
opts: Group O
Group O plasma holds anti-A and anti-B and agglutinates both A1 and B cells.
Group A
Group A plasma holds anti-B and would agglutinate the B cells, not the A1 cells.
Group B
Correct. Reverse typing reads antibodies: agglutination of A1 cells only means anti-A is present, the pattern of group B, whose plasma holds anti-A.
Group AB
Group AB plasma has no ABO antibodies and agglutinates neither reagent cell.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 11

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 45-year-old man has a febrile non-hemolytic reaction during platelets. What causes this kind of reaction?
opts: ABO IgM with complement lysis
ABO IgM with complement causes acute intravascular hemolysis with shock and red urine, not a fever with normal labs.
Stored cytokines or anti-white cell antibodies

Correct. The febrile non-hemolytic reaction has a dual cause: cytokines (interleukin-1, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor alpha) accumulated in stored plasma, and recipient antibodies against donor white cell antigens. It is commoner with platelets.
Anti-IgA in an IgA-deficient patient
Anti-IgA causes anaphylaxis with no fever, within seconds to minutes.
Recipient IgE to donor plasma proteins
Recipient IgE against soluble donor plasma proteins causes the allergic reaction: hives and itching, with no fever.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 19, 20, 17 and 21

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 50-year-old man has hives during a transfusion. What do his direct antiglobulin test and hemolysis labs show?
opts: Positive direct test, normal labs
A positive direct test marks immune coating of red cells (acute or delayed hemolysis); an allergic reaction leaves red cells alone.
Negative direct test, normal labs
Correct. Laboratory evaluation in the allergic reaction is normal: the direct antiglobulin test is negative and there are no hemolysis markers.
Positive direct test, spherocytes
A positive direct test with spherocytes is the delayed hemolytic reaction, days after transfusion.
Negative direct test, high lactate dehydrogenase
A raised LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) is a hemolysis marker; allergic reactions have none.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 20 and 22

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 48-year-old man gets hives during a platelet transfusion; it is paused and an antihistamine given, but he then begins wheezing. What should happen to the unit?
opts: Do not restart it
Correct. Critical red flag: if fever, dyspnea, wheezing or hypotension occur, do NOT restart; escalate to the full reaction protocol.
Restart it after a second dose
More antihistamine does not change the rule: wheezing is a red flag that forbids any restart.
Restart it more slowly
A slow restart is only for symptoms strictly confined to the skin that completely resolve; wheezing rules it out.
Finish it within 4 hours
A restart is allowed only for a skin-only reaction, within the 4-hour hang time; wheezing means the unit is stopped and the full protocol begins.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 20

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 59-year-old man has a transfusion reaction with fever, stable blood pressure, a negative direct antiglobulin test and clear plasma and urine. Which reaction fits?
opts: Anaphylactic
Anaphylaxis has no fever and does have shock, with stridor and a high tryptase.
Allergic
The allergic reaction has NO fever; its fingerprint is itching and hives that respond to an H1-blocker.
Acute hemolytic
The acute hemolytic reaction has fever WITH shock, a newly positive direct test and pink plasma with red urine.
Febrile non-hemolytic
Correct. Fever with no hypotension, a negative direct test and normal hemolysis labs (clear plasma and urine) is the febrile non-hemolytic fingerprint, a diagnosis of exclusion.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set1.q: A 70-year-old man transfused 6 weeks ago has a type and screen drawn. His surgery is 5 days later. What is needed before surgery?
opts: A new sample, drawn and retested

Correct. After a transfusion within the prior 3 months the sample is valid for only 72 hours (3 days), because new alloantibodies can form rapidly after secondary exposure; an expired sample needs a new draw and repeat testing.
An electronic crossmatch
A crossmatch done on an expired sample would miss a newly formed antibody; the sample itself must be redrawn.
Nothing; the sample lasts a week
His recent transfusion limits the sample to 72 hours; on day 5 it has expired.
A repeat forward type
The concern is a NEW alloantibody, which forward typing cannot find; the whole testing is repeated on a fresh sample.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 15

set1.io: Define the importance of pre-transfusion testing.
set1.q: A 61-year-old woman is starting her first unit of red cells. How should the first 25 to 50 mL be given?
opts: As a rapid bolus to check tolerance
A rapid bolus would push more incompatible blood in before a reaction is seen. As little as 25 mL can trigger a severe acute hemolytic reaction, so the start is slow.
Slowly, while she is watched closely
Correct. The first 15 minutes are critical: infuse the first 25 to 50 mL slowly, because a severe acute hemolytic reaction shows itself rapidly, after as little as 25 mL.
After routine premedication
Routine premedication is discouraged; it does not replace a slow start. The first 25 to 50 mL are infused slowly under close watch.
At the full ordered rate from the start
The full rate skips the critical first 15 minutes of vigilance. The first 25 to 50 mL go in slowly while she is watched.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 4, 17 and 19

set1.io: Review Rh factor and incompatibility.
set1.q: A 27-year-old RhD-negative woman without anti-D has abdominal trauma late in pregnancy with a large fetal-maternal bleed. Which test decides whether she needs more than the usual Rh immune globulin?
opts: Antibody identification panel
An identification panel maps the specificity of an antibody after a positive screen; she has no antibody, and it says nothing about bleed volume.
Reverse typing
Reverse typing detects her ABO antibodies with reagent A1 and B cells; it cannot quantify fetal cells in her blood.
Direct antiglobulin test
The direct antiglobulin test asks whether red cells are already coated with antibody in the body; it does not measure how much fetal blood entered the mother.
Kleihauer-Betke test
Correct. The Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies the volume of fetal-maternal hemorrhage, to calculate whether additional vials of Rh immune globulin are required.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 9, 14 and 12

set1.io: Review Rh factor and incompatibility.
set1.q: A 41-year-old woman's antibody screen is negative. Outside the ABO system, which red cell antigen is the most immunogenic?
opts: Kidd
Kidd (anti-Jka) is the classic cause of a delayed hemolytic reaction, but RhD is the most immunogenic antigen outside ABO.
Kell
Kell is a clinically significant minor antigen (anti-K is a high-risk specificity on the panel), but RhD is the most immunogenic outside ABO.
RhD
Correct. RhD is the most immunogenic red cell antigen outside the ABO system, a transmembrane protein; an Rh-negative person exposed by transfusion or pregnancy can form anti-D.
Duffy
Duffy (anti-Fya) is a high-risk minor specificity found on an identification panel; RhD is the most immunogenic outside ABO.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 8 and 12

set1.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set1.q: A 52-year-old man's type is unknown and he needs red cells before typing can be done. Which ABO group is the universal red cell donor?
opts: Group A
Group A red cells carry the A antigen and would be lysed by the anti-A of a group B or O patient.
Group AB
Group AB is the universal red cell RECIPIENT and the universal plasma donor; its red cells carry both antigens and would be lysed by anti-A or anti-B.
Group O
Correct. Group O red cells carry no A or B antigen, so recipient anti-A and anti-B have nothing to react with: O is the universal red cell donor.
Group B
Group B red cells carry the B antigen and would be lysed by the anti-B of a group A or O patient.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 6

set1.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set1.q: A 25-year-old pregnant woman has her routine prenatal antibody screen. Which test is this?
opts: Forward typing
Forward typing detects ABO antigens on her cells; the prenatal screen looks for antibodies in her plasma.
Kleihauer-Betke test
The Kleihauer-Betke test measures the volume of fetal-maternal hemorrhage; it does not screen for antibodies.
Indirect antiglobulin test

Correct. The indirect antiglobulin test (indirect Coombs) looks for free, unbound antibodies in plasma; its uses include maternal prenatal antibody screens, pre-transfusion screening and crossmatching.
Direct antiglobulin test
The direct test examines red cells already coated in the body, as in hemolytic reactions or hemolytic disease of the newborn, not a mother's free plasma antibodies.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 14 and 9

set1.io: Define the importance of pre-transfusion testing.
set1.q: A 47-year-old man is about to receive a red cell unit. The nurses check his name, medical record number, the unit's blood type and its serial number. Against what is this information matched directly?
opts: The room number on the door
A room or bay number identifies a place, not a person; the bay 1 and bay 2 mix-up is how a unit reaches the wrong patient. The match is made against the wristband.
The electronic order alone
An order says what was requested, not who is in the bed. The bedside check matches the unit and patient details directly against the wristband.
His spoken date of birth
One spoken detail is not two-identifier verification. The name, record number, unit type and serial number are matched against the wristband.
His wristband
Correct. Two-identifier verification matches the patient's name, medical record number, the unit's blood type and the unit's serial number directly against the patient's wristband at the bedside.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 4

set1.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set1.q: A 62-year-old man with a known anti-Kell needs 2 units. Which crossmatch tier takes the longest per unit?
opts: Each tier takes equal time
The tiers differ widely: under a minute, about 5 to 10 minutes, and 45 to 60 or more minutes per unit.
Immediate-spin crossmatch
Immediate spin takes about 5 to 10 minutes: mixed at room temperature and centrifuged at once.
Electronic crossmatch
The electronic crossmatch is instantaneous, under a minute, and requires a negative screen.
Full antiglobulin crossmatch

Correct. The full antiglobulin crossmatch, which he needs, takes 45 to 60 or more minutes per unit (37 °C incubation, then antihuman globulin); immediate spin takes about 5 to 10 minutes and electronic under a minute.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 13

set1.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set1.q: A 24-year-old woman of unknown blood type is bleeding heavily after a car crash and needs red cells immediately. Which units should be released?
opts: Uncrossmatched O-positive
O-positive is the massive transfusion standard for adult males and post-menopausal females. In a young woman, RhD exposure risks lifelong anti-D and fetal hydrops in future pregnancies.
Group AB-negative
Group AB red cells carry A and B antigens and would be lysed by the anti-A or anti-B of most recipients; AB is the universal plasma donor, not the red cell donor.
Uncrossmatched O-negative

Correct. O-negative is the scarce universal red cell, kept as a strict emergency reserve and mandatory for females of childbearing potential (under 50) with an unknown type, so RhD exposure cannot sensitize her.
Units after a full crossmatch
A full antiglobulin crossmatch takes 45 to 60 or more minutes per unit. In hemorrhage, emergency units are sent uncrossmatched while the blood bank confirms.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 7, 6 and 13

set1.io: Define the importance of pre-transfusion testing.
set1.q: A 56-year-old woman dies after a hemolytic transfusion reaction. Where does such a fatal reaction most often begin?
opts: A clerical error at the bedside
Correct. Human error drives mortality: most fatal hemolytic reactions stem from bedside clerical errors, not from laboratory testing. Verify the patient and the unit at the bedside.
A missed antibody on the screen

A screen that misses a weak historical antibody causes a delayed hemolytic reaction with gradual extravascular clearance, where hemodynamic collapse is rare; fatal reactions are mostly clerical ABO mismatches.
Contamination of the donor unit
Bacterial contamination is the sepsis concern when a fever is high; fatal hemolytic reactions most often come from bedside clerical errors.
A laboratory typing failure
The blood bank testing is usually accurate; the unit is delivered to the wrong patient. Laboratory failure is the exception, not the usual cause.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 24, 4 and 17

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 41-year-old man's peripheral smear is reviewed 10 days after a transfusion with a falling hemoglobin. Which smear finding fits a delayed hemolytic reaction?
opts: Blast cells
Blast cells are not a transfusion reaction finding; the smear shows spherocytes.
A normal smear
A normal smear does not fit ongoing extravascular hemolysis; spherocytes are listed among the delayed reaction labs.
Eosinophils
Eosinophils are not among the delayed reaction findings; spherocytes are.
Spherocytes

Correct. Delayed hemolysis is extravascular: splenic macrophages clear IgG-coated cells, and the peripheral smear shows spherocytes, with elevated LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) and indirect bilirubin and reduced haptoglobin.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set1.q: A 63-year-old man who types as group AB needs red cells. From which ABO groups can he receive them?
opts: AB only
AB only is his rule for PLASMA, which is the reverse: AB plasma is the only plasma without anti-A or anti-B to spare his cells. For red cells he can take any group.
AB, A, B or O
Correct. Group AB plasma has no ABO antibodies, so red cells of any ABO group are safe: AB is the universal red cell recipient.
A or B only
There is no reason to exclude group O red cells: they carry no ABO antigen, and an AB patient has no ABO antibody to react with.
O only
O only is the red cell rule for group O, whose plasma has both anti-A and anti-B. Group AB has neither antibody.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 6

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 23-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has a delayed reaction in which both the donor cells and her own red cells are destroyed and her reticulocytes fall. Why is this dangerous?
opts: It needs washed red cells next
Washed red cells strip plasma IgA for patients with anti-IgA anaphylaxis; they are not the answer to hyperhemolysis.
It needs Rh immune globulin
Rh immune globulin prevents anti-D after pregnancy events; it does not treat hyperhemolysis.
It will resolve with antihistamine
An antihistamine treats the skin-limited allergic reaction; hyperhemolysis is destruction of her own cells too.
More transfusion can be fatal
Correct. Hyperhemolysis syndrome: the antibodies destroy BOTH donor and autologous red cells, reticulocytopenia develops, and further transfusions can be fatal.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 18, 21, 20 and 9

set1.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set1.q: A 31-year-old woman types as group B. Which enzyme gives her red cells their ABO antigen?
opts: N-acetylgalactosamine transferase
N-acetylgalactosamine transferase belongs to group A and makes the A antigen. Group B uses D-galactosyltransferase.
D-galactosyltransferase
Correct. Group B possesses D-galactosyltransferase and group A possesses N-acetylgalactosamine transferase; group O shows only the unmodified H core, with no A or B sugars.
A transmembrane D protein
The D antigen is the Rh system's transmembrane protein, not an ABO enzyme. Group B possesses D-galactosyltransferase.
No transferase
No transferase fits group O, which shows only the unmodified H core with no A or B sugars. Group B possesses D-galactosyltransferase.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 5 and 8

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 31-year-old woman with severe IgA deficiency and anti-IgA survived transfusion anaphylaxis. What must she receive for future transfusions?
opts: Leukoreduced red cells
Leukoreduction removes white cells to prevent febrile reactions; it leaves plasma IgA in the product.
Washed red cells
Correct. Future transfusions must be washed red cells, which strips the plasma IgA, or products sourced from verified IgA-deficient donors.
Routine premedication
Premedication does not remove the IgA that triggers her reaction; only washing or IgA-deficient donors do.
Group AB plasma
Group AB plasma is the universal plasma donor for ABO, but it still contains IgA.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 21, 19 and 6

set1.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set1.q: A 60-year-old woman's temperature rises 2.3 °C during a platelet transfusion and her blood pressure falls. Beyond the hemolysis workup, what must be investigated?
opts: A delayed hemolytic reaction
A delayed hemolytic reaction appears 3 to 30 days later, rarely with hemodynamic collapse.
Bacterial sepsis from the product
Correct. Rule out sepsis: if the fever is 2 °C or more, the patient is hypotensive, or the product was platelets, work up for bacterial sepsis (blood bag Gram stain and culture). She has all three.
A new anti-Kell antibody
A new minor-antigen antibody causes delayed extravascular hemolysis, not a high fever with hypotension during platelets.
An allergic reaction to plasma
An allergic reaction has no fever and no hypotension; her high fever with hypotension during platelets raises sepsis.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 19 and 18

set1.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set1.q: A 40-year-old man receives ABO-incompatible red cells and his cells lyse inside the circulation within minutes. Which antibody class drives this?
opts: IgE
IgE mediates the allergic reaction against donor plasma proteins: hives and itching, with normal hemolysis labs.
IgA
Donor IgA is the trigger of anaphylaxis in a recipient who lacks IgA and has anti-IgA; it is not the ABO antibody.
IgG
IgG is the Rh (anti-D) and minor-antigen class: monomers that coat cells for splenic clearance, a gradual extravascular course, not lysis in the circulation within minutes.
IgM
Correct. ABO antibodies are IgM: large pentamers that are highly efficient at fixing complement (C1q binding), so the membrane attack complex lyses cells directly in the circulation.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 5 and 10

set1.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set1.q: A 44-year-old woman has a negative antibody screen, no history of significant antibodies, and only one blood type record on file. Which crossmatch fits?
opts: Immediate-spin crossmatch

Correct. Immediate spin needs a negative screen with no history of clinically significant antibodies; her serum is mixed with donor cells at room temperature and centrifuged at once, in about 5 to 10 minutes.
A direct antiglobulin test
The direct antiglobulin test checks for antibody already coating her cells in the body; it is not a crossmatch tier.
Full antiglobulin crossmatch
The full antiglobulin crossmatch is for a positive screen or a history of significant antibodies; she has neither.
Electronic crossmatch
The electronic crossmatch needs at least two concordant blood type records; she has only one.
set1.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 13 and 14

mis.Electronic crossmatch: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set2.q: A 70-year-old man who is RhD-negative receives O-positive red cells during a massive transfusion. Which risk is specific to giving him RhD-positive cells?
opts: A febrile reaction from cytokines
Stored cytokines cause febrile reactions with any unit; the specific risk of RhD-positive cells in an RhD-negative man is anti-D formation.
Immediate intravascular hemolysis
He has no anti-D at baseline (Rh-negative people have zero pre-existing anti-D), so there is no immediate hemolytic collapse.
Later formation of anti-D
Correct. An Rh-negative man given O-positive cells will NOT suffer immediate intravascular hemolysis. Alloimmunization (anti-D) may occur, but surviving the hemorrhage takes precedence.
Anaphylaxis from donor IgA
Anaphylaxis from donor IgA needs a severely IgA-deficient recipient with anti-IgA; it has nothing to do with the RhD antigen.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 7 and 8

mis.Immediate intravascular hemolysis: reversed rule (Rh has no natural antibody)

set2.io: Define the importance of pre-transfusion testing.
set2.q: A 52-year-old woman needs a blood sample drawn for pre-transfusion testing. How should the sample tube be labeled?
opts: At the bedside, in front of her
Correct. Label the sample immediately at the bedside in front of the patient. Mislabeled samples (wrong blood in tube) are a root cause of fatal ABO reactions.
Pre-labeled before the blood draw
Tubes are never pre-labeled. A tube labeled before the draw can be filled from the wrong patient, the classic wrong-blood-in-tube error behind fatal reactions.
At the nursing station afterward
Labeling away from the patient is exactly what the safety protocol forbids; the label goes on at the bedside, in front of the patient, right after the draw.
By the blood bank when it arrives
The blood bank cannot know whose blood is in an unlabeled tube. Labeling happens immediately at the bedside in front of the patient.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 4

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 62-year-old woman's acute hemolytic reaction is followed by falling urine output. Which renal laboratory pattern is expected?
opts: Rising creatinine, low potassium
Creatinine rises, but so does potassium: hyperkalemia is listed with the renal labs.
Rising creatinine and potassium
Correct. Renal labs show a rising urea nitrogen and serum creatinine with hyperkalemia, from free hemoglobin causing tubular injury (acute tubular necrosis).
Falling creatinine and potassium
Kidney injury raises creatinine, and hyperkalemia is part of the acute hemolytic renal picture.
Normal creatinine, low potassium
Normal kidney labs do not fit acute tubular necrosis from free hemoglobin; creatinine and potassium both rise.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 17 and 5

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 30-year-old woman who was pregnant 2 months ago has a pre-transfusion sample drawn. Why is it valid for only 3 days?
opts: The red cells hemolyze in the tube
The rule is immunologic, not about the tube: a new antibody may appear after recent exposure.
Her ABO group may change
Her ABO group does not change; the concern is a newly formed alloantibody against other red cell antigens.
New antibodies can form quickly
Correct. A pregnancy within the prior 3 months limits the sample to 72 hours: new alloantibodies can form rapidly following secondary exposure, so the sample must reflect her current plasma.
Rh immune globulin expires
Rh immune globulin timing is a separate pregnancy rule; the 3-day limit is about new alloantibodies.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 15

set2.io: Define the importance of pre-transfusion testing.
set2.q: A 34-year-old man in one trauma bay is given a red cell unit meant for the patient in the next bay. Within 5 minutes he has rigors, flank pain, low blood pressure and dark urine. The blood bank had typed both patients correctly. What caused this reaction?
opts: An undetected minor-antigen antibody
A missed antibody against a minor antigen such as Kidd causes a delayed reaction days later, with gradual extravascular clearance, not shock within 5 minutes of the wrong unit.
An error in forward typing
Both patients were typed correctly, so the laboratory did not fail here. The lesson of this case is that human error at the bedside, not laboratory failure, drives fatal reactions.
Cytokines stored in the unit
Stored cytokines cause a febrile non-hemolytic reaction with stable blood pressure and normal laboratory results, not flank pain, shock and dark urine within minutes.
Misidentification at the bedside

Correct. The blood bank testing was accurate, but the unit reached the wrong patient. Fatal ABO incompatibility is almost always clerical: a mislabeled sample (wrong blood in tube) or a failed two-person check at the bedside.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 4 and 17

mis.An error in forward typing: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Review Rh factor and incompatibility.
set2.q: A 28-year-old RhD-negative woman made anti-D after delivering an RhD-positive first baby. She is now carrying a second RhD-positive fetus. How does her antibody reach the fetus?
opts: Fetal cells enter her bloodstream
Fetal cells entering her circulation (feto-maternal hemorrhage) is how she was SENSITIZED; harm to the fetus comes from her IgG crossing back.
IgM anti-D crosses the placenta
Anti-D is IgG (mainly IgG1 and IgG3), a monomer that crosses the placenta; IgM is the large ABO pentamer.
Complement crosses the placenta
It is her IgG antibody that crosses, through Fc receptors; the fetal cells are then destroyed in the spleen.
IgG anti-D crosses the placenta

Correct. In later pregnancies maternal IgG anti-D crosses the placenta through syncytiotrophoblast Fc receptors, binds fetal red cells and causes splenic destruction: hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 9 and 10

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 60-year-old man who was transfused 2 years ago is typed before surgery. Which test would find an unexpected anti-Kell in his plasma?
opts: Forward typing
Forward typing detects the A and B antigens on his red cells; it does not look for antibodies at all.
Electronic crossmatch
The electronic crossmatch is software checking ABO and Rh compatibility, and it requires a NEGATIVE screen first.
Direct antiglobulin test
The direct antiglobulin test asks whether his red cells are already coated in the body; free antibodies in plasma are the screen's job.
Antibody screen

Correct. The antibody screen is an indirect antiglobulin test that identifies unexpected circulating IgG alloantibodies against clinically significant red cell antigens, such as Kell, Duffy, Kidd and Rh antigens.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 12, 11 and 13

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 67-year-old man's antibody screen is positive. What is the next laboratory step?
opts: Release of O-negative units
Uncrossmatched O-negative is an emergency release in hemorrhage, not the routine answer to a positive screen.
An antibody identification panel
Correct. When the screen is positive, an 11- to 16-cell panel is tested to map the specific antibody specificity, so antigen-negative donor units can be found.
A Kleihauer-Betke test
The Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetal-maternal hemorrhage for Rh immune globulin dosing; it does not identify an alloantibody.
An electronic crossmatch
An electronic crossmatch requires a negative screen; a positive screen calls for identification and a full antiglobulin crossmatch.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 12, 13 and 9

mis.An electronic crossmatch: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set2.q: A 36-year-old woman who types as group B needs red cells. From which ABO groups can she receive them?
opts: B or AB
B or AB is her rule for PLASMA. Group AB red cells carry the A antigen, which her anti-A would attack.
Any ABO group
Any group is the red cell rule for group AB only. Her anti-A would lyse group A and AB cells.
B only
Group O red cells are also safe: they carry no A or B antigen, which is why group O is the universal red cell donor.
B or O
Correct. Her plasma holds anti-A, so red cells carrying A (groups A and AB) are excluded; group B cells match and group O cells carry no ABO antigen.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 6

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 57-year-old woman with a negative screen gets an immediate-spin crossmatch. What is its purpose?
opts: To detect weak IgG to minor antigens
Detecting weak IgG binding against minor antigens is the purpose of the full antiglobulin crossmatch, with 37 °C incubation.
To identify a new alloantibody
Identifying an antibody's specificity is the job of the 11- to 16-cell panel after a positive screen.
A final check of ABO compatibility
Correct. Immediate spin is the final serologic check to confirm ABO compatibility and rule out a clerical mismatch; it does not look for weak IgG binding.
To find coating on her own cells
Antibody already coating her own cells in the body is what the direct antiglobulin test finds.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 13, 12 and 14

set2.io: Review Rh factor and incompatibility.
set2.q: A 46-year-old man with anti-D receives RhD-positive cells. Which course is expected?
opts: Gradual, with mild jaundice

Correct. Rh hemolysis is extravascular and gradual: spherocytes, mild hyperbilirubinemia and low haptoglobin, or an asymptomatic drop in hemoglobin. It rarely triggers acute shock or disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Stridor within seconds
Stridor within seconds is anaphylaxis, classically from anti-IgA in an IgA-deficient recipient.
Shock within minutes
Shock within minutes is the ABO pattern: IgM and complement lysing cells in the circulation. Rh reactions are gradual.
Hives without fever
Hives without fever is the allergic reaction to donor plasma proteins, with normal hemolysis labs.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 8 and 10

set2.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set2.q: A 38-year-old woman who types as group O needs plasma. From which ABO groups can she receive it?
opts: O only
O only is her rule for RED CELLS, because her plasma holds anti-A and anti-B. For plasma the logic inverts: any group is safe for her.
AB only
AB only is the plasma rule for a group AB patient, whose cells carry both antigens. Group O cells carry neither.
A or B only
Group O plasma and group AB plasma are just as safe for her: her cells have no A or B antigen for any donor antibody to attack.
O, A, B or AB
Correct. Plasma rules run the opposite way to red cells: group O cells carry no A or B antigen, so no donor plasma antibody can attack them. Group O is the universal plasma recipient.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 6

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 33-year-old woman develops itching hives 30 minutes into a fresh frozen plasma transfusion, with no fever, wheezing or change in vital signs. The infusion is paused and an antihistamine given, and the hives fully resolve. What can be done with the unit?
opts: Switch her to washed red cells
Washed red cells are for patients with anti-IgA anaphylaxis; her reaction was skin-limited and resolved.
Restart it at a faster rate
The restart is at a SLOWER rate, and within the 4-hour hang time limit.
Restart the same unit more slowly

Correct. The exclusive restart rule: if symptoms stay strictly confined to the skin and completely resolve, the SAME unit may be restarted at a slower rate within the 4-hour hang time limit. No other reaction allows a restart.
Discard it; reactions never restart
A purely skin-limited allergic reaction that resolves is the one exception: the same unit may be restarted slowly.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 20 and 21

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 74-year-old man has had febrile non-hemolytic reactions before. Which measure most reduces their rate?
opts: Routine premedication
Routine premedication is discouraged; removing the white cells before storage is what prevents these reactions.
Pre-storage leukoreduction

Correct. Pre-storage leukoreduction dramatically reduces febrile non-hemolytic reactions, which come from cytokines accumulated in stored plasma and from recipient antibodies against donor white cell antigens.
IgA-deficient donors
IgA-deficient donor products are for patients with anti-IgA anaphylaxis, not for febrile reactions.
Washed red cells
Washed red cells strip plasma IgA for patients with anti-IgA anaphylaxis.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 19 and 21

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman's transfusion is stopped for a suspected reaction. What happens to the remaining blood bag and tubing?
opts: The unit is kept for later use
A unit implicated in a reaction is returned for testing, not kept; only a skin-limited allergic reaction allows a restart of the same unit.
The bag is flushed into her
Remaining blood is never flushed into the patient; it goes back to the blood bank.
They are discarded at the bedside
Discarding them destroys the evidence; the bag and tubing are returned for testing and cultures.
They go back to the blood bank
Correct. Send the remaining product, the intact tubing and all attached tags back to the blood bank for testing and cultures.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 57-year-old man had a negative antibody screen before his transfusion, yet a delayed hemolytic reaction follows. Why did the screen miss it?
opts: The unit was the wrong ABO group
An ABO mismatch causes an acute hemolytic reaction within minutes, not a delayed one days later.
His old antibody was undetectable
Correct. The anamnestic trap: a historical antibody had fallen below detection on the pre-transfusion screen, and re-exposure to the donor antigen stimulated rapid IgG production.
The screen does not detect IgG
The screen is built to detect IgG alloantibodies; it missed this one because it had fallen too low to detect.
He made natural IgM to Kidd
Naturally occurring IgM is the ABO pattern; the delayed reaction is a secondary IgG response to a minor antigen such as Kidd.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 18 and 12

set2.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set2.q: A 44-year-old man becomes hypotensive and shocked minutes into an ABO-incompatible transfusion. Which products of the reaction cause the vasodilation?
opts: Free hemoglobin in the tubules
Free hemoglobin causes the kidney injury (tubular precipitation and acute tubular necrosis), not the vasodilation; that comes from C3a and C5a.
Anti-IgA antibodies
Anti-IgA causes anaphylaxis in an IgA-deficient recipient; an ABO mismatch works through complement and its anaphylatoxins.
The anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a
Correct. In the intravascular cascade, the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a cause systemic vasodilation, hypotension and shock.
Recipient IgE to plasma proteins
Recipient IgE against donor plasma proteins is the allergic reaction, which has no hypotension by definition.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 5, 20 and 21

set2.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set2.q: A 26-year-old woman with trauma and an unknown blood type is given O-negative rather than O-positive units. What future harm does this choice prevent?
opts: Acute intravascular hemolysis now
RhD-positive cells cause no immediate intravascular hemolysis in an unsensitized RhD-negative patient. The harm prevented is anti-D and fetal hydrops later.
Fetal hydrops in later pregnancies

Correct. Exposure to RhD in a young female risks lifelong anti-D formation and fetal hydrops in future pregnancies, so O-negative is mandatory for females of childbearing potential with an unknown type.
An allergic reaction to plasma
Allergic reactions come from recipient IgE against donor plasma proteins; the RhD status of red cells does not prevent them.
A febrile non-hemolytic reaction
Febrile reactions come from stored cytokines or anti-white cell antibodies and are reduced by pre-storage leukoreduction, not by RhD-negative units.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 7 and 9

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 46-year-old woman's polyspecific direct antiglobulin test is positive. What is done next with the sample?
opts: Retest with anti-IgG and anti-C3d
Correct. The direct test uses polyspecific antihuman globulin (anti-IgG plus anti-C3d); if positive, it is tested with monospecific anti-IgG and anti-C3d to see what is coating the cells.
Repeat it with reagent A1 cells
Reagent A1 and B cells belong to reverse typing of ABO antibodies, not to sorting out a positive direct test.
Send it for a Kleihauer-Betke
The Kleihauer-Betke test measures fetal-maternal hemorrhage; it does not sort IgG from complement on red cells.
Add 37 °C incubation to it
Incubation at 37 °C is part of the full antiglobulin crossmatch and the indirect test, where antibody is attached in vitro.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 14 and 13

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 47-year-old woman reacts within seconds after only 2 mL of a blood product. Which reaction does this timing suggest?
opts: Febrile non-hemolytic reaction
The febrile reaction falls during or within 4 hours of transfusion, with a fever and stable vital signs.
Delayed hemolytic reaction
A delayed hemolytic reaction appears 3 to 30 days after transfusion.
Allergic urticaria
Allergic urticaria comes during or within 4 hours, confined to the skin with no shock.
Anaphylaxis
Correct. Anaphylaxis comes on suddenly, within seconds to minutes, after only 1 to 5 mL of product; the classic cause is anti-IgA in a severely IgA-deficient patient.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 21 and 22

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 61-year-old woman's reaction workup shows a newly positive direct antiglobulin test. Which two reactions can produce this?
opts: Acute and delayed hemolytic

Correct. A newly positive direct antiglobulin test is the hallmark of immune hemolysis: positive in the acute and the delayed hemolytic reactions, negative in the febrile, allergic and anaphylactic reactions.
Febrile and anaphylactic
The febrile reaction and anaphylaxis both have a negative direct test with normal hemolysis labs; neither coats red cells.
Febrile and allergic
The febrile and allergic reactions both have a negative direct test and normal hemolysis labs; neither puts antibody on red cells.
Allergic and anaphylactic
Both have a negative direct test; they are driven by IgE or anti-IgA, not by antibody on red cells.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 22 and 24

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman's plasma agglutinates neither reagent A1 cells nor reagent B cells. What is her ABO group?
opts: Group O
Group O plasma holds both antibodies and agglutinates both A1 and B cells; no reaction is the opposite result.
Group AB
Correct. No agglutination of either reagent cell means no anti-A and no anti-B in the plasma: group AB.
Group B
Group B plasma holds anti-A and would agglutinate the A1 cells.
Group A
Group A plasma holds anti-B and would agglutinate the B cells.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 11

set2.io: Compare and contrast ABO blood groups and compatibility.
set2.q: A 1-year-old girl who has never been transfused types as group A and already has anti-B in her plasma. What triggered this antibody?
opts: Fetal-maternal bleeding at birth
Fetal-maternal hemorrhage is how a mother is sensitized to RhD, which needs exposure. ABO antibodies need none: gut flora and food carbohydrates prime them in infancy.
Gut flora and food sugars in infancy
Correct. ABO antibodies are naturally occurring: they form without prior transfusion, primed during infancy by cross-reactive gut flora and food carbohydrates.
An earlier transfusion
She has never been transfused. ABO antibodies form without any transfusion; that is what naturally occurring means.
A vaccine containing B antigen
No vaccine is involved. ABO antibodies are naturally occurring, triggered in infancy by cross-reactive gut flora and food carbohydrates.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 5 and 8

mis.An earlier transfusion: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 58-year-old man's plasma agglutinates both reagent A1 cells and reagent B cells. What is his ABO group?
opts: Group AB
Group AB is the opposite reverse pattern: no agglutination of either cell, because AB plasma has no ABO antibodies.
Group B
Group B plasma holds only anti-A, so it agglutinates A1 cells only.
Group O
Correct. In reverse typing, agglutination of both A1 and B cells means anti-A and anti-B are both present: group O.
Group A
Group A plasma holds only anti-B, so it agglutinates B cells only.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 11

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 64-year-old man's forward type reads group A, but his reverse type reads group O. What should happen before blood is released?
opts: Hold release and investigate
Correct. Forward and reverse types MUST match before blood is released; any discrepancy prompts immediate investigation.
Accept the reverse type
Neither half overrides the other: the forward and reverse types must agree before any blood goes out.
Release group AB plasma
The rule is about the ABO type itself: forward and reverse must match, and a discrepancy is investigated before any blood is released.
Release group A units
Trusting one half of a discrepant type risks an ABO mismatch; nothing is released until the two agree.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 11

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman develops chills and a fever 10 minutes into a red cell transfusion. What is the first action?
opts: Give acetaminophen and continue
Acetaminophen treats a febrile non-hemolytic reaction, which is a diagnosis of exclusion; first the blood is stopped and hemolysis ruled out.
Flush the line with saline
Flushing would push the remaining blood into her. The line is kept open with new tubing and fresh saline, never flushed.
Stop the transfusion

Correct. For any suspected reaction, stop the infusion immediately; do not slow the rate. A mild fever early on could be a benign febrile reaction or the first sign of a fatal acute hemolytic reaction.
Slow the infusion rate
Slowing still infuses blood that may be incompatible; the rule is to halt the transfusion, not slow it.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 16 and 19

set2.io: Review Rh factor and incompatibility.
set2.q: A 25-year-old RhD-negative woman with no anti-D is pregnant. When is routine Rh immune globulin given during the pregnancy?
opts: At about 28 weeks of gestation

Correct. Routine prophylaxis with Rh immune globulin is given at about 28 weeks of gestation to all non-sensitized RhD-negative mothers, with a post-partum dose within 72 hours of delivering an RhD-positive baby.
Once her screen turns positive
Rh immune globulin prevents sensitization; it is for NON-sensitized mothers, so it is given before any anti-D appears.
In her next pregnancy
Prophylaxis is given in this pregnancy, at about 28 weeks, to every non-sensitized RhD-negative mother.
After the first delivery
Waiting for delivery misses the routine antenatal dose at about 28 weeks; the post-partum dose is a second dose, not the only one.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Discuss laboratory testing used in transfusion medicine.
set2.q: A 71-year-old man has a positive antibody screen. Which crossmatch must be used?
opts: Reverse typing
Reverse typing reads the ABO antibodies; it does not crossmatch donor units against a non-ABO antibody.
Immediate-spin crossmatch
Immediate spin also requires a negative screen; it only confirms ABO compatibility and would miss weak IgG binding.
Full antiglobulin crossmatch

Correct. A positive screen or a documented history of clinically significant antibodies requires the full antiglobulin crossmatch: 37 °C incubation, then antihuman globulin, to detect weak IgG binding against minor antigens.
Electronic crossmatch
The electronic crossmatch requires a negative screen; his is positive.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 13 and 11

mis.Electronic crossmatch: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.Immediate-spin crossmatch: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with transfusion reactions.
set2.q: A 45-year-old man's plasma and urine are inspected after a suspected reaction. Which appearance points to an acute hemolytic reaction?
opts: Pink plasma and red urine
Correct. Visual inspection in an acute hemolytic reaction shows pink or red plasma (hemoglobinemia) and red urine (hemoglobinuria), from free hemoglobin released by lysed cells.
Clear plasma and clear urine
Clear plasma and urine are the normal findings of the febrile non-hemolytic, allergic and anaphylactic reactions.
Clear plasma, then jaundice later
Mild jaundice days later with spherocytes is the gradual extravascular course of a delayed hemolytic reaction.
Cloudy plasma from fat
Fat in plasma is not a transfusion reaction finding; hemolysis turns the plasma pink or red.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 17 and 22

set2.io: Define the importance of pre-transfusion testing.
set2.q: A 29-year-old man has no verified blood type on record and now needs a transfusion. His first sample has been typed. What is required to confirm his ABO and Rh type?
opts: Group O-negative units are mandatory
Uncrossmatched O-negative is an emergency release for hemorrhage, not the routine answer to a missing type. A second separate sample confirms his type.
The first tube is typed twice
Retesting the same tube cannot catch wrong blood in tube; a mislabeled first sample gives the same wrong answer twice. A separate second sample is drawn.
An electronic crossmatch replaces it
An electronic crossmatch needs at least two concordant blood type records on file, which he does not have. The second sample is what creates the confirmation.
A second, separate sample is tested
Correct. The second-sample rule: if the patient has no prior verified blood type on record, a second separate sample must be drawn and tested to confirm the ABO and Rh type.
set2.cite: 21. Transfusion Medicine Blood Banking Fundamentals SV.pptx, Slides 4 and 13
